doc.title: Charles McPherson interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 9, 2024 [interview 2 of 2]

chapter: Changes in jazz and advice to young players
title: How jazz has changed since the sixties
summary: McPherson sees more genres and offshoots of jazz now, similar musicianship, and a big change in school jazz programs.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: This is a sort of a tough question but you’ve been involved in jazz for a long time. We spoke about your time with Charles Mingus and having your own bands all these years. And then you just spoke about playing a jazz festival like three weeks ago in Upstate New York. Can you think about the biggest changes you’ve noticed in jazz and the business of jazz between that time back in the sixties and now?

Well yeah, that’s — I think there — you know I think there might be more genres of jazz maybe now than before. In the sixties you had the influence of Charlie Mingus, people like John Coltrane, the avante garde was happening you know, Ornette was there. You had you know Art Blakey and of course Thelonious Monk, Max Roach, you had these great musicians that were still here and everybody had their own style but I think now the difference is there just might be more different offshoots of jazz. Or people that play or record companies that promote and they’ll use the term jazz you know, and there are just more variations I would say. Maybe a little more variations. In terms of the aesthetic of it,

I mean the actual quality and level of musicianship and artistry, you know the sixties and even before that had very high levels of musicianship and artistry you know. That didn’t start with the sixties, that’s always been around. And now you — I’ll tell you what is different, academia is different. There are more schools — high schools, colleges — that have jazz programs. That wasn’t quite like that in the sixties and of course earlier. So that’s different, so therefore it’s producing younger players, you know there’s a lot of young people that are enamored of jazz, some kind of jazz, and it’s in the schools and so it’s more available in a way, at least by way of academia. And so that’s a little different, and it produces, you know, a slew of young players that are being, you know that are getting out of schools, that are starting careers. So there might be, maybe more people playing jazz and yeah — so things have changed but to answer your question the best way I can I would say that there’s more genres now maybe, and a lot more players you know.
